content: Order Centrales, a traditional classification within the heterokont algae group known as diatoms, is characterized by the unique morphology of its cell walls, also referred to as valves or frustules. The valves of centric diatoms are typically circular or ellipsoid when observed in valve view. These structures often exhibit radially symmetrical ornamental patterns, which, under an optical microscope, may appear as dots. Additionally, some centric diatoms possess spines on their valves. These spines can serve dual purposes: they may increase the cell's surface area, thereby reducing its sinking rate, or they may function as a defense mechanism against predation by zooplankton. A distinguishing feature of centric diatoms is the absence of a raphe, a slit-like structure present in pennate diatoms. Regarding their cell cycle, the vegetative cells of centric diatoms are diploid and undergo mitosis during routine cell division. In species that reproduce sexually, oogamous meiosis occurs, resulting in the production of haploid gametes, which are either ova or sperm cells. The fusion of these gametes forms a zygote, which subsequently enlarges to develop into an auxospore. The auxospore then gives rise to fully developed vegetative cells. In certain taxonomic classifications, centric diatoms are alternatively referred to as Order Coscinodiscophyceae.
